title: How to Halve or Double a Cupcake Recipe
summaryShort: To halve or double a cupcake recipe, scale every ingredient by weight, split eggs by whisking and weighing, and keep the bake time close to the original. Use one muffin pan for a half batch and two for a double.
metaTitle: How to Halve or Double a Cupcake Recipe
metaDescription: Learn how to halve a cupcake recipe or double it with a simple scaling table, egg splitting tips, and pan counts. Read the guide and bake with confidence.
sidebarBullets: Weigh ingredients in grams for the cleanest math.
Half an egg is about 25 g, or 1 1/2 tbsp beaten egg
Scale baking powder and soda by the same ratio as flour.
Keep the same bake time, but check 2 minutes early.
Use a hand mixer for small batches and a 5 qt bowl for doubles.

sections.heading: Can You Simply Multiply Every Ingredient?
paragraphs: Yes, cupcake recipes scale well because the ratios stay the same when you multiply everything by the same number. A half batch is every ingredient times 0.5, and a double batch is times 2.
The trouble comes from awkward amounts, like half an egg or 1/8 teaspoon. Those small amounts are where most home bakers go wrong, so I plan them before I start.
list: Halve: multiply by 0.5.
Double: multiply by 2.
Write the new amounts on paper before measuring.
Convert cups to grams first if your recipe lists them.

sections.heading: How Do You Split an Egg Exactly?
paragraphs: Whisk the egg until the yolk and white are fully blended, then weigh it and use half. One large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, so half is about 25 g, or 1 1/2 tablespoons.
Pour the leftover half into a small jar, cover it, and refrigerate it. Use it within a day in scrambled eggs or to brush on bread.
list: Crack the egg into a small bowl.
Whisk until the streaks disappear.
Weigh it, then pour out half by weight.
If your scale is not exact enough, use 1 1/2 tablespoons

sections.heading: How Do You Scale Baking Powder and Soda?
paragraphs: Scale leavening by the same ratio as the flour, and use true measuring spoons. Half of 1 teaspoon is 1/2 teaspoon, and half of 1/2 teaspoon is 1/4 teaspoon.
For 1/4 teaspoon baking soda, a half batch needs 1/8 teaspoon, so level a 1/4 teaspoon and scoop out half. A pinch too much gives a bitter, soapy taste and a dome that collapses.
list: Too much leavening: domed tops that sink, coarse crumb, bitter taste.
Too little: dense, pale, and short cupcakes.
For doubles, scale up straight, but add a scant 1/4 teaspoon less if you go beyond triple

sections.heading: Why Does Baking Time Barely Change?
paragraphs: Baking time stays almost the same because each cupcake is still the same size. Heat has to travel through the same depth of batter, no matter how many cupcakes are in the oven.
A half batch can finish about 1 to 2 minutes sooner because the oven is less crowded. A double batch in two pans can need 1 to 2 extra minutes, so I check at the early end of the range.
list: Test with a toothpick at the minimum time.
Look for a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.
Do not change the oven temperature.

sections.heading: What Mixer Bowl Size Do You Need?
paragraphs: A 5 quart stand mixer bowl handles a double batch of most cupcake batters comfortably. A 4.5 quart bowl works, but it fills up fast and splashes flour.
Half batches have the opposite problem, because the paddle may miss butter at the bottom of a big bowl. I use a hand mixer in a medium bowl and scrape often.
list: Double batch: 5 quart bowl or larger.
Half batch: medium bowl and hand mixer.
Scrape the bowl twice during mixing.

sections.heading: How Many Pans and What Goes in Each Cup?
paragraphs: A standard recipe fills one 12-cup pan, so a double batch needs two pans. A half batch fills six cups, and the empty cups should hold a little water to stop the pan from warping.
Fill each liner about two-thirds full. Bake the pans on the center rack one at a time, or swap racks halfway if you bake both together.
list: Half batch: 6 cups filled, 6 cups with a splash of water.
Original: 1 pan of 12.
Double: 2 pans of 12, rotated halfway.

howToSteps: Decide your scale factor: 0.5 for half, 2 for double.
Convert every ingredient to grams and multiply by the factor.
Whisk any egg that needs splitting, then weigh and use half.
Scale baking powder, baking soda, and salt with the same factor.
Pick the right bowl and mixer for the new batch size.
Fill liners two-thirds full and add water to empty pan cups.
Bake at the original temperature and test 2 minutes early.

faq.question: How do I halve a recipe that calls for one egg?
faq.answer: Whisk the egg, weigh it, and use about 25 g, or 1 1/2 tablespoons. Refrigerate the rest, covered, and use it within a day.

faq.question: Can I triple a cupcake recipe the same way?
faq.answer: You can, but you will need a large mixer bowl and three pans. Mix in one bowl only if it holds the batter with room to spare, or make two batches.

faq.question: Do I need to change the oven temperature for a double batch?
faq.answer: No. Keep the same temperature and swap pan positions halfway so both pans brown evenly.

faq.question: Why did my half batch cupcakes turn out flat?
faq.answer: The leavening was probably measured too lightly or not scaled exactly. Use a 1/8 teaspoon measure and level it carefully.

faq.question: Is it better to make two single batches instead of one double?
faq.answer: A double works fine for most butter cakes in a 5 quart bowl. Two single batches are safer for delicate batters like chiffon or whipped egg white cakes.
